nodes.label: Electronics
nodes.blurb: Reading a schematic, driving a microcontroller, not letting the smoke out.

nodes.label: Soldering
nodes.blurb: Through-hole, then surface mount, then the fine pitch that ruins your evening.

nodes.label: Painting
nodes.blurb: Brush, rattle can, airbrush. The skill that decides whether a model reads as finished.

nodes.label: Photography
nodes.blurb: Light, exposure, and the patience to shoot the same thing twenty times.

nodes.label: Programming
nodes.blurb: Enough code to make a thing you built do something you wanted.

nodes.label: 3D Printing
nodes.blurb: Modelling, slicing, and the long argument with adhesion.

nodes.label: Hand Tools
nodes.blurb: Cutting, filing, drilling and gluing, plus the jig that makes the second one match the first.

nodes.label: Audio
nodes.blurb: Capturing sound in a room that fights you, then cleaning it up afterwards. No edit rescues a bad recording.

nodes.label: Writing
nodes.blurb: The build log, the script and the caption. What turns a thing you made into a thing somebody else can follow.

nodes.label: Gunpla
nodes.blurb: Bandai's snap-fit Gundam kits. No glue needed to start, no ceiling if you keep going.

nodes.label: Scale Armour
nodes.blurb: Tanks at 1/35. Glue, putty and reference photos, where gunpla gives you none of the three.

nodes.label: Aircraft Kits
nodes.blurb: Canopies, camouflage masks and the long argument about panel line scale.

nodes.label: Dioramas
nodes.blurb: A base, a scene and a reason the model is standing where it is.

nodes.label: Airbrush Rig
nodes.blurb: Compressor, moisture trap, spray booth. The purchase that changes what finishes are possible.

nodes.label: Decals
nodes.blurb: Waterslides, setting solution and the silvering that gives away a rushed job.

nodes.label: Layout Building
nodes.blurb: Planning and building the railway itself. The people who finish a small one keep the hobby; the people who plan a huge one sell it on in two years.

nodes.label: Scale and Gauge
nodes.blurb: N, HO, OO, O, G. The first decision, and in practice the only irreversible one, because every purchase after it assumes the answer.

nodes.label: Benchwork
nodes.blurb: The physical table the whole hobby sits on. Level, rigid, and reachable at the back, or you will regret all three.

nodes.label: Trackwork
nodes.blurb: Where reliability is won or lost. Bad joints and tight radii cause more frustration in this hobby than everything else combined.

nodes.label: Layout Wiring
nodes.blurb: Power bus, feeders and block sections. An intermittent fault does not read as a fault, it reads as a locomotive that stalls for no reason.

nodes.label: DCC
nodes.blurb: Digital Command Control. Every locomotive gets an address, so two trains share one track and neither one cares.

nodes.label: Decoder Install
nodes.blurb: Fitting a decoder inside a shell. Surface-mount work in a space the size of a thumbnail, on a model you already paid for.

nodes.label: Locomotives
nodes.blurb: The motorised part. Brass, plastic or kit-built, and the one component where the price of running well is obvious.

nodes.label: Rolling Stock
nodes.blurb: Cars and wagons, bought or kitbashed. Metal wheels and working couplers are the two upgrades everyone eventually makes to all of them.

nodes.label: Structure Building
nodes.blurb: Styrene, laser-cut wood and card. The buildings that tell you what decade and which country the railway is in.

nodes.label: Scenery
nodes.blurb: Foam, plaster, static grass and poured water. The layer that turns a track plan into a place.

nodes.label: Weathering Stock
nodes.blurb: Rust, brake dust and sun fade. It is the single change that stops a layout photographing like a toy.

nodes.label: Operating Sessions
nodes.blurb: Running the railway to a timetable with waybills and a dispatcher, so the trains have somewhere to be rather than just going round.

nodes.label: Prototype Research
nodes.blurb: Studying the real railway you are modelling. Archives, track diagrams and a lot of photographs of things nobody else photographs.

nodes.label: Railfanning
nodes.blurb: Watching and filming the full-size railway. A different hobby that happens to share a subject, and a lot of people do both.

nodes.label: Onboard Cab Camera
nodes.blurb: A wireless camera small enough to sit inside a locomotive cab. The shot nobody can get any other way.

nodes.label: Modular Clubs
nodes.blurb: A standard module spec so twenty people's sections bolt together at a show. How you get a huge layout without owning a huge room.

nodes.label: MOC Building
nodes.blurb: My Own Creation. Building something that never came in a box, using only parts that exist, which is a harder constraint than it sounds.

nodes.label: Lego Trains
nodes.blurb: Motorised trains on plastic track at roughly L gauge. A layout hobby with a parts bin instead of a paint booth.

nodes.label: SNOT Technique
nodes.blurb: Studs Not On Top. Turning bricks sideways to get surfaces and angles the system was not obviously designed for.

nodes.label: Digital Design
nodes.blurb: Building the model in software first, with a parts list that comes out the other end. You find out what it costs before you buy it.

nodes.label: Publishing Instructions
nodes.blurb: Turning your own build into steps somebody else can follow. Step order is a genuine design problem and most first attempts fail it.

nodes.label: Technic
nodes.blurb: Beams, pins, gears and linkages. Where the system stops being a surface and starts being a mechanism.

nodes.label: Powered Motors
nodes.blurb: Motors, hubs and a bluetooth app, or a third-party controller if you want the model to do something the app will not.

nodes.label: Robotics Sets
nodes.blurb: Sensors, motors and a block or text programming environment. Many people's first program made something physical move.

nodes.label: Ball Contraptions
nodes.blurb: Modules that pass balls to each other at a fixed rate, built to a shared standard so strangers' machines connect at a show.

nodes.label: Brick Dioramas
nodes.blurb: A scene rather than a model. Landscaping in a medium with no curves, which is exactly the interesting part.

nodes.label: Fan Shows
nodes.blurb: Club tables at a convention centre, where the modular standards pay off and everybody's section joins up.

nodes.label: Set Collecting
nodes.blurb: Sealed, built or retired. A collecting hobby with a published catalogue and a secondary market that watches it closely.

nodes.label: Minifigure Collecting
nodes.blurb: The small yellow people, including the licensed ones. Cheap to start, deep to specialise, easy to fake.

nodes.label: Parts Sourcing
nodes.blurb: Buying by element and colour rather than by set. The skill that separates people who build from a bin from people who build a design.

nodes.label: Sorting and Storage
nodes.blurb: By part, by colour, or by neither. The unglamorous decision that decides whether building is a pleasure or a search.

nodes.label: Miniature Painting
nodes.blurb: Painting something 32mm tall so it reads correctly from two feet away. The most transferable painting skill on the map.

nodes.label: Garage Kits
nodes.blurb: Unpainted resin, usually a limited run, usually of an anime character. A collector expects an assembly job and discovers a refinishing job.

nodes.label: Printed Minis
nodes.blurb: Resin printing your own. The supply problem disappears and a support-removal problem arrives in its place.

nodes.label: Bases and Plinths
nodes.blurb: The ground the figure stands on, and half of what a judge is actually looking at. A good base can carry an average figure.

nodes.label: Batch Painting
nodes.blurb: Sixty models to one standard, in an order that never puts the brush down twice. A different skill from painting one well.

nodes.label: Display Busts
nodes.blurb: Head and shoulders at a scale where every brushstroke is visible. Where painters go to work on skin and eyes.

nodes.label: Painting Contests
nodes.blurb: Cabinet judging against a standard nobody writes down. The fastest feedback in the hobby and the least gentle.

nodes.label: Custom Repaints
nodes.blurb: Stripping a factory paint job off a mass-produced figure and doing it properly. Cheap practice on a good sculpt.

nodes.label: Sculpting
nodes.blurb: Epoxy putty over an armature, or digital sculpting for print. The step from finishing someone's design to having one.

nodes.label: Moulding and Casting
nodes.blurb: Silicone, resin and a pressure pot. Becoming the garage in garage kit, along with a real ventilation problem.

nodes.label: Figure Photography
nodes.blurb: Macro, a backdrop and an eye-level camera. Shooting a figure from above makes it look like a toy on a desk, which it is.

nodes.label: Figure Collecting
nodes.blurb: Scale literacy, brands, release cycles and the shelf that ran out two years ago.

nodes.label: Scale Figures
nodes.blurb: Prepainted PVC at 1/7 and 1/8, sold on preorder eighteen months before it exists. The mainstream of the hobby.

nodes.label: Articulated Figures
nodes.blurb: Poseable lines with swappable hands and faces. Bought to be posed and photographed rather than left in the box.

nodes.label: Bootleg Literacy
nodes.blurb: Recasts and counterfeits are a real market, and telling one apart is a learned skill involving box print, paint slop and seam lines.

nodes.label: Display and Lighting
nodes.blurb: Cabinets, UV, dust and LED strips. The point where a collection stops being storage and becomes a presentation.

nodes.label: Warhammer
nodes.blurb: Assemble it, paint it, then lose with it. Two thirds of the hobby happens at a desk on your own before anything happens on a table.

nodes.label: Tabletop RPGs
nodes.blurb: Four people, some dice and a shared story that only exists while everyone is at the table. The cheapest entry on this whole map.

nodes.label: Skirmish Games
nodes.blurb: Ten models instead of a hundred. The format that lets someone finish a force, which is the format most people should start with.

nodes.label: Terrain Building
nodes.blurb: Foam, card and sprue offcuts turned into ruins to fight over. A table of painted armies on bare board still looks unfinished.

nodes.label: Historical Wargaming
nodes.blurb: Real battles at scale, with rules arguing about frontage and morale. Where the research is half the pleasure.

nodes.label: List Building
nodes.blurb: Building a force inside a points budget. A puzzle you can play for an hour without opening a box.

nodes.label: Tournaments
nodes.blurb: Five games in a weekend against strangers. The deadline that finally gets an army painted.

nodes.label: Setting and Lore
nodes.blurb: The novels, the codices and forty years of accumulated background. Plenty of people are only here for this.

nodes.label: Running a Game
nodes.blurb: Preparation, pacing and improvising when the players do the thing you did not write. A performance skill wearing a hobby's coat.

nodes.label: Game Design
nodes.blurb: Writing rules that survive contact with people trying to win. Playtesting is where the design actually happens.

nodes.label: Print and Play
nodes.blurb: A PDF, a printer and an evening with a craft knife. How most designs get tested before anyone spends money.

nodes.label: Dice and Accessories
nodes.blurb: Sets, trays, towers and the sharp-edged resin ones. A small collecting hobby attached to every game in this cluster.

nodes.label: Card Games
nodes.blurb: Constructed decks, draft nights and a secondary market that behaves like a small stock exchange.

nodes.label: Board Games
nodes.blurb: Everything from forty minutes to a full Saturday. The gateway most of this cluster arrives through.

nodes.label: Solo Play
nodes.blurb: Games designed for one, and campaigns played against a deck instead of an opponent. What the hobby does when nobody is free.

nodes.label: Mecha Anime
nodes.blurb: Giant robots, sixty years of them, and the design lineage that explains why the kit on your shelf looks the way it does.

nodes.label: Manga
nodes.blurb: The source most series are adapted from, usually longer, usually different, and usually still running.

nodes.label: Seasonal Watching
nodes.blurb: Following a cour as it airs, one episode a week, with everybody else watching the same episode that day.

nodes.label: Anime Films
nodes.blurb: Two hours, one budget, and the format most likely to convince somebody who says they do not watch anime.

nodes.label: Pre-2000 Anime
nodes.blurb: Cel-era work, hand-painted and shot on film. Looks nothing like what came after, and increasingly hard to see properly.

nodes.label: Studios and Staff
nodes.blurb: Following key animators, directors and studios rather than titles. Turns a watch list into something with a shape.

nodes.label: Subs and Dubs
nodes.blurb: Translation, localisation and the twenty-year argument. Comparing two scripts of the same scene teaches more than either one alone.

nodes.label: Learning Japanese
nodes.blurb: The point where a viewer stops waiting for a translation. A years-long commitment that a hobby talked somebody into.

nodes.label: Art Books
nodes.blurb: Settei sheets, colour scripts and mechanical designs. Reference material for anybody building or drawing the thing.

nodes.label: Production Cels
nodes.blurb: Hand-painted acetate from the pre-digital era. A real archival hobby, with real forgeries and real conservation problems.

nodes.label: Drawing in the Style
nodes.blurb: Studying construction, expression sheets and how a face is built. Copying badly for a long time is the documented method.

nodes.label: Doujinshi and Fanwork
nodes.blurb: Self-published fan work, printed in small runs and sold at events. An entire parallel publishing culture.

nodes.label: Conventions
nodes.blurb: Panels, dealer halls and the queue. Where the online half of this hobby turns into people standing in a room.

nodes.label: Merchandise
nodes.blurb: Standees, keychains, tapestries and the endless small goods. Cheap individually, ruinous cumulatively.

nodes.label: Anime Music
nodes.blurb: Openings, endings and the composers who score whole seasons. Often the first thing somebody keeps after dropping a show.

nodes.label: Horror
nodes.blurb: The genre with the deepest subgenre map and the most committed people arguing about it. You can like several of them and dislike the rest.

nodes.label: Physical Media
nodes.blurb: Boutique labels, restorations and the transfer that finally looks the way it did in a cinema. Owning it because streaming keeps removing it.

nodes.label: Science Fiction
nodes.blurb: From the model-and-motion-control era to whatever is rendered now. The genre most likely to send a viewer to a workbench.

nodes.label: Kaiju and Tokusatsu
nodes.blurb: Suit actors, miniature cities and pyrotechnics. Practical effects taken to their most committed conclusion.

nodes.label: Animation
nodes.blurb: Cel, stop motion and everything after. A medium the rest of the shelf keeps mistaking for a genre.

nodes.label: Noir and Crime
nodes.blurb: Low key lighting, worse people, and a run of films short enough that you can actually see most of it.

nodes.label: Documentary
nodes.blurb: The genre that most often turns a viewer into a participant, because somebody on screen is doing something you could do.

nodes.label: Film History
nodes.blurb: Watching by director, movement or decade instead of by whatever is on. The point where a habit becomes a subject.

nodes.label: Logging and Lists
nodes.blurb: Recording what you watched and what you thought. A hobby's memory, and the reason you can tell what a year actually looked like.

nodes.label: Writing About Film
nodes.blurb: Four hundred words that make somebody watch a film they had dismissed. Harder than it looks, and cheap to try.

nodes.label: Festivals
nodes.blurb: Watching four in a day with people who chose the same four. Where the recommendations for the next year come from.

nodes.label: Soundtracks
nodes.blurb: Scores on vinyl and the composers people follow across films. A second collection that grows out of the first.

nodes.label: Home Cinema
nodes.blurb: Projector, screen, speakers and a room you can make properly dark. The gear rabbit hole attached to the watching.

nodes.label: Film Projection
nodes.blurb: Running actual 16mm or 35mm at home. A mechanical repair hobby wearing a film hobby's coat.

nodes.label: Practical Effects
nodes.blurb: Miniatures, animatronics, latex and squibs. Studying how the shot was faked is one short step from building props yourself.

nodes.label: YouTube Channel
nodes.blurb: Cadence, retention and a title somebody clicks. The craft that decides whether anyone sees the other ten things you learned.

nodes.label: Video Editing
nodes.blurb: Cut, pace, structure. Where a boring twenty minutes becomes an interesting six, and where every mistake made while filming becomes permanent.

nodes.label: Videography
nodes.blurb: Camera, tripod, slider and the decision about where to put all four. Coverage you did not shoot cannot be edited in later.

nodes.label: Lighting a Scene
nodes.blurb: Key, fill and something behind the subject. Miniatures in particular need far more light than your eyes suggest they do.

nodes.label: Audio Capture
nodes.blurb: Microphone placement and a room that is not helping. No edit recovers a bad recording, which is why this sits before the edit and not after it.

nodes.label: Voiceover
nodes.blurb: Reading your own script without sounding like you are reading your own script. Recorded after the cut, so it fits the pictures.

nodes.label: Scripting
nodes.blurb: Deciding what the video is about before the camera is out. The cheapest place to fix a video is the page.

nodes.label: Thumbnails and Titles
nodes.blurb: One frame and six words. Unfair, unavoidable, and the part most makers refuse to take seriously until they do.

nodes.label: Colour Grading
nodes.blurb: Matching shots to each other first, and only then giving the whole thing a look. In that order, always.

nodes.label: Motion Graphics
nodes.blurb: Titles, diagrams and callouts that move. The difference between showing a wiring diagram and explaining one.

nodes.label: Macro and Stacking
nodes.blurb: At model scale, depth of field is the whole problem. Focus stacking is how a 1/87 scene ends up sharp front to back.

nodes.label: Timelapse
nodes.blurb: The build compressed to forty seconds. Cheap to shoot, unforgiving about a camera that moved on day three.

nodes.label: Live Streaming
nodes.blurb: No edit, no retake, and a chat that asks the question you were about to answer. A different nerve from recorded video.

nodes.label: Short Form
nodes.blurb: Under a minute, vertical, and it has to work with the sound off. Reaches people who would never open a twenty minute build log.

nodes.label: Podcasting
nodes.blurb: Two people, two microphones and a subject deep enough to last an hour. The lowest gear cost of anything in this cluster.

nodes.label: Prop Replicas
nodes.blurb: Building the object rather than buying it. A hilt, a blaster, a helmet, accurate to the frame it appeared in.

nodes.label: Pixel Saber
nodes.blurb: An addressable-LED saber with a soundboard inside the hilt. The cheapest board demands the most skill, which is the opposite of what people expect.

nodes.label: Saber Config Files
nodes.blurb: ProffieOS config editing. C-style syntax, blade styles as expressions, and the real skill gate on the open-source board.

nodes.label: Sound Fonts
nodes.blurb: Hum, clash, swing and ignition, each a separate file the board picks from. Half of what makes a saber feel real is heard, not seen.

nodes.label: Blade Assembly
nodes.blurb: Polycarbonate tube, foam diffuser, tip and epoxy. Wrong-gauge wire on the data line gives you a segment that sticks.

nodes.label: Hilt Machining
nodes.blurb: Turning aluminium on a lathe, or assembling a CNC hilt kit. The part people actually hold has to feel dense.

nodes.label: Chassis Design
nodes.blurb: The printed skeleton that holds board, battery and speaker still inside a tube that gets hit. Tolerances decide whether it rattles.

nodes.label: Saber Choreography
nodes.blurb: Forms, footwork and contact drills. It is also the stress test that finds every solder joint you rushed.

nodes.label: Costuming
nodes.blurb: Armour, soft parts and a costume judged against reference photos by a club that will tell you what is wrong with it.

nodes.label: Conventions
nodes.blurb: Where a shelf becomes a conversation. Also where the person who solved your problem three years ago is standing.

nodes.label: The Films and Series
nodes.blurb: Nine films, the animation, the live-action series. The reference library everything else in this cluster is checked against.

nodes.label: Books and Comics
nodes.blurb: Novels, comics and the visual dictionaries that name the greeblie you are trying to identify.

nodes.label: Vintage Figures
nodes.blurb: Kenner 3.75 inch figures from 1977 onward. Provenance, cardback variants and the reproduction accessories that fool people.

nodes.label: Star Wars Model Kits
nodes.blurb: Bandai runs this line on the same tooling as its Gundam kits, so the snap-fit habits transfer whole.

nodes.label: Prop Photography
nodes.blurb: A lit blade in a dark room is a long exposure problem. The glow is the shot, and the shot is what people see.

nodes.label: Ham Radio
nodes.blurb: Licensed amateur radio. An exam, a callsign, and permission to talk to a stranger on another continent with equipment you can fix yourself.

nodes.label: Meshtastic
nodes.blurb: An off-grid LoRa mesh on licence-free ISM spectrum. One board and one antenna is the whole entry cost, and no exam stands in front of it.

nodes.label: Node Building
nodes.blurb: Picking a board and getting firmware onto it. ESP32 for the web interface, nRF52 when the node has to run for weeks on a cell.

nodes.label: Mesh Configuration
nodes.blurb: Region and modem preset have to match across the whole mesh or a node that looks fine talks to nobody. Region is also the legal envelope.

nodes.label: Solar Repeater
nodes.blurb: A node on a mast that nobody visits. Solar budget, weatherproofing, mounting and the site access conversation that comes before all three.

nodes.label: Antennas
nodes.blurb: Wire, tube and maths. Never key a transmitter without one attached, because the reflected power goes back into the chip.

nodes.label: Propagation
nodes.blurb: Why the same rig reaches Japan at 3am and nothing at noon. Solar flux, the ionosphere, and grey-line timing.

nodes.label: Digital Modes
nodes.blurb: FT8, packet and APRS. Contacts made at signal levels a human ear cannot hear, which is where ham thinking and mesh thinking meet.

nodes.label: SDR Listening
nodes.blurb: A dongle the price of a takeaway turns a laptop into a receiver across most of the spectrum. Listening first, transmitting later.

nodes.label: Satellite Passes
nodes.blurb: Amateur birds and the ISS repeater pass overhead for about ten minutes. You track, you correct for doppler, and then it is gone.

nodes.label: HF Station
nodes.blurb: The step from a handheld to a desk: a transceiver, a tuner, a feedline and enough garden for an antenna that resonates.

nodes.label: POTA and SOTA
nodes.blurb: Parks and Summits on the Air. Carry a light station somewhere with a view, make contacts from it, then write the activation up.

nodes.label: Contesting
nodes.blurb: A weekend of making as many contacts as possible under one set of rules. It is the fastest way to find out what your station cannot do.

nodes.label: QSL Cards
nodes.blurb: The postcard that confirms a contact happened. A hundred-year-old habit that turned a hobby into a shoebox worth keeping.

nodes.label: Morse Code
nodes.blurb: Not required for any current licence class, and still the mode that gets through when voice cannot. Learned by ear, not by table.

nodes.label: Arduino
nodes.blurb: A cheap board, a C-ish dialect and a library for almost everything. The place most people's electronics actually starts, and the toolchain a surprising number of hobbies quietly use.

nodes.label: Addressable LEDs
nodes.blurb: One data line, hundreds of individually coloured pixels. One dead pixel stops the data there and everything after it sticks, and counterfeit strips are common enough to check for.

nodes.label: ESP32 and RP2040
nodes.blurb: Boards with wifi, bluetooth or two cores for the price of a sandwich. Where a project stops being a circuit and starts being a device.

nodes.label: Sensors
nodes.blurb: Temperature, distance, current, orientation. Reading the world is easy; trusting the number you get back is the actual skill.

nodes.label: Batteries and Power
nodes.blurb: Cells, protection circuits and buck converters. A protected 18650 ships around 3.7 volts, but a tripped protection board reads zero, which looks to a beginner like a dead cell.

nodes.label: Soldering Bench
nodes.blurb: Temperature-controlled iron, flux, braid, hot air and light you can actually see by. The bench is most of the difference between joints that hold and joints that look like they hold.

nodes.label: Test Gear
nodes.blurb: Multimeter, bench supply, logic analyser, scope. Debugging without them is guessing with extra steps.

nodes.label: PCB Design
nodes.blurb: Schematic capture, layout, gerbers, and a fab that ships you five boards for the price of a pizza.

nodes.label: Repair and Teardown
nodes.blurb: Recapping, reflowing and reading a board you have no schematic for. The cheapest way to get good at soldering is fixing things nobody wants.

nodes.label: Robotics
nodes.blurb: Motors, drivers and a control loop. The first project where the software being wrong makes a noise.

nodes.label: Wearable Electronics
nodes.blurb: Circuits that have to survive being worn: flexible wire, connectors that unplug, and a battery somebody can reach.

nodes.label: Home Automation
nodes.blurb: Local sensors and local control, without a subscription and without a cloud that can be switched off.

nodes.label: CAD Modelling
nodes.blurb: Parametric sketching, and the discipline of designing a part around the tolerance of the machine that will make it.

nodes.label: Printer Tuning
nodes.blurb: Flow, temperature towers, retraction and a first layer you can trust. A tuned cheap printer beats an untuned expensive one.

nodes.label: Enclosure Design
nodes.blurb: The box. Heat inserts, screw bosses, cable strain relief, and the lid that comes off again when you need it to.

nodes.label: Laser and CNC
nodes.blurb: Subtractive machines. Flat stock, a toolpath, extraction, and the smell that tells your neighbours what you are doing.

nodes.label: Custom Keyboards
nodes.blurb: Switches, keycaps, lube and firmware. An input device rebuilt as a hobby, where the sound of a keypress is a spec you tune on purpose.

nodes.label: FPV Flying
nodes.blurb: Goggles on, flying from the aircraft's point of view. Closer to a motor skill than a gadget, and it takes real hours before it stops being terrifying.

nodes.label: Cinematic Drone
nodes.blurb: Smooth, slow and planned, for footage that goes in an edit rather than on a highlight reel. A different aircraft and a different discipline from racing.

nodes.label: Simulator Practice
nodes.blurb: Crashing for free. The one piece of consensus advice in this hobby is to spend hours here before spending money on props.

nodes.label: Freestyle
nodes.blurb: Flowing lines through gaps and around structures. Judged by feel, and the reason most people bought the goggles.

nodes.label: Drone Racing
nodes.blurb: Gates, a timer and other people. Repair skill matters as much as flying skill because everybody crashes.

nodes.label: Tiny Whoops
nodes.blurb: Ducted micro quads light enough to fly indoors. Cheap, survivable, and the fastest way to accumulate flight hours.

nodes.label: Building a Quad
nodes.blurb: Frame, motors, stack, camera and a lot of small solder joints that vibrate for a living.

nodes.label: Flight Controller Tuning
nodes.blurb: PID rates, filters and firmware flags. The software half, where a build that flies becomes a build that flies well.

nodes.label: LiPo Safety
nodes.blurb: Charge rates, storage voltage, a bag, and never a swollen pack. The one part of this hobby that can set fire to a house.

nodes.label: Field Repair
nodes.blurb: A soldering iron in a car boot. Everybody crashes, so the flying session lasts as long as your ability to fix things does.

nodes.label: Video Link and Antennas
nodes.blurb: Analogue or digital, 5.8 GHz, and antennas whose polarisation actually matters. Radio work by another name.

nodes.label: Rules and Licensing
nodes.blurb: Registration, categories, altitude limits and where you may not fly. Ignorance of this is what closes flying sites for everybody else.

nodes.label: Aerial Photography
nodes.blurb: Stills from an angle nobody used to be able to afford. Light and weather decide the day more than the aircraft does.

nodes.label: Mapping and Survey
nodes.blurb: Flying a grid and turning the overlap into an orthomosaic or a model. The point where a hobby turns into a service somebody pays for.

nodes.label: Astrophotography
nodes.blurb: Hours of exposure on something that moves, then hours of processing. The results people share are the output of a whole night and a whole evening after it.

nodes.label: Visual Observing
nodes.blurb: Looking through the eyepiece rather than photographing. Cheaper, harder to share, and the version that keeps people out under the sky.

nodes.label: Telescopes
nodes.blurb: Aperture, focal ratio and mount capacity. The scope that gets used is the one you can carry outside without thinking about it.

nodes.label: Building a Scope
nodes.blurb: A Dobsonian from plywood, or grinding a mirror by hand over months. The oldest maker tradition in this cluster.

nodes.label: Star Hopping
nodes.blurb: Finding a faint object by navigating from bright stars with a chart. A real navigational skill that survives the battery going flat.

nodes.label: Solar Observing
nodes.blurb: The one target available in daylight, through a filter that must never fail. Sunspots and flares change hour to hour.

nodes.label: Meteor Watching
nodes.blurb: No equipment at all beyond a chair and a blanket. The lowest cost of entry anywhere on this map.

nodes.label: Satellite Spotting
nodes.blurb: Predicting a pass and watching it cross. Same tables, same doppler thinking as the people talking through those satellites.

nodes.label: Tracking Mounts
nodes.blurb: Equatorial tracking, polar alignment and periodic error. The mount decides what the camera can do, not the telescope.

nodes.label: Autoguiding
nodes.blurb: A second small camera watching one star and nudging the mount. The step where imaging stops fighting you.

nodes.label: Stacking and Processing
nodes.blurb: Hundreds of frames averaged into one, then stretched. More of the final image is made here than at the telescope.

nodes.label: Planetary Imaging
nodes.blurb: Thousands of video frames, the sharpest few percent kept. Beats the atmosphere by sampling faster than it wobbles.

nodes.label: Deep Sky
nodes.blurb: Nebulae and galaxies, faint enough that light pollution decides what is possible before the equipment does.

nodes.label: Dark Sky Sites
nodes.blurb: Driving somewhere with no streetlights, often with other people. Half of astronomy skill is site selection and weather reading.

nodes.label: Synthesizers
nodes.blurb: Oscillators, filters and envelopes. An instrument you learn by understanding the signal path rather than by practising scales.

nodes.label: Vinyl Collecting
nodes.blurb: Pressings, matrix numbers and the shop you go to on a Saturday. A research hobby that happens to make noise.

nodes.label: Eurorack
nodes.blurb: A synthesiser you assemble from modules and patch by hand. Deep, expensive, and it never reaches a state you would call finished.

nodes.label: DIY Guitar Pedals
nodes.blurb: A through-hole kit in an enclosure you drill yourself. The classic first electronics build with an audible reward at the end.

nodes.label: Guitar
nodes.blurb: The instrument most people already have in a cupboard. Everything downstream in this cluster tends to plug into it.

nodes.label: Music Theory
nodes.blurb: Names for what your ear already noticed. Not required to play, and it makes everything faster once you have it.

nodes.label: Playing Live
nodes.blurb: A room, a set and equipment that has to work first time. The fastest way to find out which parts you actually know.

nodes.label: Home Recording
nodes.blurb: Interface, microphones and a DAW. The room is the instrument nobody budgeted for, and it decides more than the microphone does.

nodes.label: Mixing
nodes.blurb: Balance, then space, then tone. Mostly a listening skill trained by comparing your work against records you know.

nodes.label: Sampling
nodes.blurb: Taking a fragment and making it yours. Chopping, pitching, and the clearance question nobody wants to answer.

nodes.label: Field Recording
nodes.blurb: A recorder, a windshield and somewhere interesting. Trains, machinery, weather and rooms, captured because nobody else did.

nodes.label: Chiptune
nodes.blurb: Music written for sound chips with three or four voices. Real constraints, and often written on the original hardware.

nodes.label: DJing
nodes.blurb: Selection first, mixing second. Reading a room is the part no equipment upgrade helps with.

nodes.label: Hi-Fi
nodes.blurb: Amplifiers, speakers and room treatment, plus a lively argument about which of the three actually matters.

nodes.label: Piano
nodes.blurb: Eighty-eight keys and nowhere to hide. The instrument where theory stops being abstract, because the whole keyboard is the diagram.

nodes.label: Retro Consoles
nodes.blurb: Hardware from before online updates existed, which means it either works or it needs somebody with an iron. Increasingly that somebody is the owner.

nodes.label: CRT Displays
nodes.blurb: The display these machines were designed for, and the only one where their output looks correct. Heavy, finite in supply, and dangerous inside.

nodes.label: Arcade Cabinets
nodes.blurb: A full cabinet in a room that was not designed for one. Woodwork, a monitor, a power supply and artwork, all restorable and all heavy.

nodes.label: Pinball
nodes.blurb: Electromechanical or solid state, and either way a maintenance hobby with a game attached. Switches, coils and a lot of rubber.

nodes.label: Console Modding
nodes.blurb: Region switches, RGB output, optical drive emulators. Fine-pitch soldering onto a board you cannot buy another of.

nodes.label: Recapping
nodes.blurb: Replacing electrolytic capacitors before they leak and eat the traces underneath. The single most useful repair skill in this cluster.

nodes.label: Cartridge Collecting
nodes.blurb: Boxed, loose or complete. A market with published price guides, regional variants and a lot of counterfeits.

nodes.label: Repro Detection
nodes.blurb: Telling a reproduction cartridge from an original by label print, board revision and the screws holding the shell together.

nodes.label: Handhelds
nodes.blurb: The cheapest way into the hobby, and the one with the most active modding scene: screens, batteries and backlights.

nodes.label: Emulation
nodes.blurb: Software that pretends to be the hardware. Accuracy versus speed is a real argument with real answers per system.

nodes.label: Vintage Computers
nodes.blurb: Eight-bit and sixteen-bit machines with documented hardware, which is why people can still write new software for them.

nodes.label: Disk Preservation
nodes.blurb: Reading decaying magnetic media at flux level before it becomes unreadable. Archival work with a real deadline.

nodes.label: Demoscene
nodes.blurb: Making a machine do something its designers said it could not, in a fixed size, and showing it at a party.

nodes.label: Mechanical Keyboards
nodes.blurb: Switches, plates, foam and a soldering iron. A modern hobby that borrowed its whole aesthetic and half its tooling from this cluster.

nodes.label: Action RPGs
nodes.blurb: Loot, seasons and a passive tree with thousands of nodes. Played by people who enjoy the spreadsheet at least as much as the fighting.

nodes.label: Build Crafting
nodes.blurb: Planning a character on a huge skill tree before playing it. The hobby of reading a graph, which is roughly what this whole site is.

nodes.label: Roguelikes
nodes.blurb: Runs rather than saves. Losing is content, and the knowledge you keep between attempts is the actual progression.

nodes.label: Strategy Games
nodes.blurb: Turn based or grand. Long sessions, deep systems, and a community that writes more documentation than the developer did.

nodes.label: Speedrunning
nodes.blurb: Route planning, frame-level execution and a timer. A performance discipline built on top of somebody else's game.

nodes.label: Game Preservation
nodes.blurb: Dumping, documenting and keeping playable the things that are no longer sold. An archival hobby with a legal grey area attached.

nodes.label: Game Modding
nodes.blurb: Editing somebody's game with their tools, or without them. The most common first programming project people actually finish.

nodes.label: Game Development
nodes.blurb: Making a small one rather than modding a big one. Scope control is the whole skill and almost nobody has it on the first try.

nodes.label: Playing With Friends
nodes.blurb: The scheduled evening that keeps a friend group in contact. Often the only hobby on this map with a fixed weekly slot.

nodes.label: Controller Modding
nodes.blurb: Hall effect sticks, arcade sticks and custom buttons. A soldering hobby that hides inside a gaming one.

nodes.label: PC Building
nodes.blurb: Parts picking, cable routing and thermals. Assembling is the easy half; deciding what to buy is where the research goes.

nodes.label: Sim Racing
nodes.blurb: Wheel, pedals and a rig bolted together. The gear escalation is steep and the physics knowledge transfers to a real track.

nodes.label: Flight Simulation
nodes.blurb: Procedures, charts and a cockpit built out of switch panels. Closer to a study hobby than to a game.

nodes.label: In-Game Photography
nodes.blurb: Composition, focal length and light inside a rendered world. Every skill transfers except the walking around.

nodes.label: JRPGs
nodes.blurb: Sixty-hour stories, turn-based menus and a party you pick favourites from. The backlog is the real endgame, and everyone in the genre is losing to it.

nodes.label: Fighting Games
nodes.blurb: Frame data, spacing and a training mode that never lies. The one genre where improvement is measured against a person who is trying to stop you.

nodes.label: Rhythm Games
nodes.blurb: Notes fall and you hit them on time, graded to the millisecond. Practice looks exactly like playing, which no instrument has managed.

nodes.label: Online Worlds
nodes.blurb: One persistent world, thousands of strangers and a raid calendar. The only games on this map that carry on without you while you sleep.

nodes.label: VR and Simulation
nodes.blurb: A headset, a cleared floor and a cable you learn to step over. Nobody believes it until the demo, and nobody explains it well afterwards either.

nodes.label: Armour Building
nodes.blurb: Plate that fits a real body rather than the drawing's body. The pattern is the hard part, the material is a preference.

nodes.label: EVA Foam
nodes.blurb: Floor mats, a sharp knife and contact cement. The cheapest route into armour and still the one most people use for anything large.

nodes.label: Thermoplastics
nodes.blurb: Sheet that goes soft with heat and holds a shape when it cools. Expensive per sheet, forgiving in a way foam is not.

nodes.label: Printed Props
nodes.blurb: Printed in sections, glued, then sanded through grits until nobody can tell. The sanding is most of the work and none of the fun.

nodes.label: Casting for Costume
nodes.blurb: Silicone moulds and resin or foam casts. What you do when you need six of a thing, or a lighter version of a heavy one.

nodes.label: Patterning
nodes.blurb: Getting a flat shape that becomes the right curved shape on a specific person. Paper mock-ups first, always, and twice if it is a helmet.

nodes.label: Sewing
nodes.blurb: Machine and hand. The soft parts nobody photographs and everybody notices when they are wrong.

nodes.label: Wig Styling
nodes.blurb: Cutting, thinning, heat setting and enough product to hold a silhouette all day. A separate craft with its own tools.

nodes.label: Makeup and Prosthetics
nodes.blurb: Contouring, body paint and appliances. Painting on a surface that sweats, moves and has to be able to blink.

nodes.label: Costume Weathering
nodes.blurb: Scuffs, grime and burn marks so a costume looks lived in rather than bought. The same technique a model gets, at ten times the scale.

nodes.label: Costume Lighting
nodes.blurb: LEDs, a battery you can reach and wiring that survives being sat down in. The first electronics project many costumers ever do.

nodes.label: Wearability
nodes.blurb: Strapping, ventilation, vision and how you get to a toilet. The thing that decides whether a finished costume is ever worn twice.

nodes.label: Cosplay Competition
nodes.blurb: Craftsmanship judging and a stage presentation. Judges look at the inside of the costume, which is a shock the first time.

nodes.label: Cosplay Photography
nodes.blurb: A location, a photographer and a character. Most of what the internet sees of this hobby is this step, not the eight weeks before it.

nodes.label: Espresso
nodes.blurb: Nine bars, twenty-five seconds and a dozen variables that all interact. The most equipment-dependent way to make a small drink.

nodes.label: Home Roasting
nodes.blurb: Green beans, heat and a curve you log. The step where the hobby stops being about buying well and starts being about doing something.

nodes.label: The Grinder
nodes.blurb: The upgrade that changes the cup more than the machine does, which is the single most repeated piece of advice in this hobby.

nodes.label: Dialling In
nodes.blurb: Dose, yield and time, changed one at a time. Scales and a timer turn guessing into something you can repeat tomorrow.

nodes.label: Water Chemistry
nodes.blurb: Hardness, alkalinity and what your tap actually contains. The invisible ingredient that is most of the drink by mass.

nodes.label: Milk Texturing
nodes.blurb: Air first, then roll. Texture is decided in the first two seconds, and everything after that is only heating.

nodes.label: Latte Art
nodes.blurb: A visible test of whether the milk was right. Not decoration so much as a scoreboard for the previous step.

nodes.label: Machine Modding
nodes.blurb: PID temperature control, pressure profiling and a flow gauge. An electronics project hiding inside a kitchen appliance.

nodes.label: Descaling and Repair
nodes.blurb: Gaskets, screens, scale and a spare parts diagram. These machines are repairable, which is why old ones stay in use.

nodes.label: Pour Over
nodes.blurb: A dripper, a filter and a kettle. Almost no equipment cost and almost all of the same variables to learn.

nodes.label: Cold Brew
nodes.blurb: Twelve hours and a jar. The method with the widest margin for error and the lowest attention cost.

nodes.label: Green Bean Sourcing
nodes.blurb: Origin, process, varietal and harvest year. A research habit that arrives about a week after the roaster does.

nodes.label: Cupping and Tasting
nodes.blurb: A standard method for tasting several coffees side by side, and the vocabulary to say what the difference actually was.

nodes.label: Cafe Hunting
nodes.blurb: Drinking other people's work on purpose. The cheapest calibration available for everything you do at home.

nodes.label: Fiction
nodes.blurb: Novels, and the pile of them beside the bed. The to-be-read stack grows faster than the read one, and everyone here pretends that is fine.

nodes.label: Nonfiction
nodes.blurb: History, memoir, science and the odd doorstop biography. The section where one good book quietly assigns you four more.

nodes.label: Sci-Fi and Fantasy
nodes.blurb: Series that run to ten volumes and worlds with appendices. The genre shelf most likely to come with a map inside the cover.

nodes.label: Comics and Graphic Novels
nodes.blurb: Single issues, trades and the long boxes that follow. Reading them is cheap; keeping them in order is the actual hobby.

nodes.label: Poetry
nodes.blurb: Short to read and slow to finish. The one shelf where reading a page four times is the method, not a failure.

nodes.label: Book Collecting
nodes.blurb: First editions, dust jackets and the difference a printing line makes. Condition grading arrives quietly and never leaves.

nodes.label: Bookbinding
nodes.blurb: Folding signatures, sewing them and casing the block in board and cloth. Starts as repairing one loved paperback, ends as a bone folder you have opinions about.

nodes.label: Annotation and Marginalia
nodes.blurb: Pencil in the margins, tabs on the edges and an index of your own in the back. A private conversation with the author, kept in the object.

nodes.label: Book Clubs
nodes.blurb: One book, one month, several people who read it differently. Half the value is being made to finish; the other half is the argument.

nodes.label: Audiobooks
nodes.blurb: Books read to you while your hands do something else. A narrator can rescue a book or sink it, which print never has to answer for.

nodes.label: Zines
nodes.blurb: Photocopied, folded, stapled and traded. Publishing with the gatekeeping removed and the staples showing.

nodes.label: Libraries and Archives
nodes.blurb: The one place the whole cluster is free. Regulars learn the catalogue, the sales shelf and the librarians by name.

nodes.label: Rereading
nodes.blurb: Going back on purpose, sometimes annually. The book did not change, which is exactly how you can tell that you did.

nodes.label: Reading in Translation
nodes.blurb: The same book exists twice, and the translator decided which one you got. Comparing editions is the enthusiast tell.

nodes.label: Houseplants
nodes.blurb: A pothos, then a monstera, then a humidifier and grow lights. The windowsill fills up before anyone admits a collection has started.

nodes.label: Vegetable Garden
nodes.blurb: Beds, seed packets and a July glut of courgettes. The supermarket is cheaper, which was never the point.

nodes.label: Herbs
nodes.blurb: Basil on the sill, rosemary by the door. The smallest possible garden that still changes what dinner tastes like.

nodes.label: Bonsai
nodes.blurb: Wiring, pruning and repotting on a schedule measured in years. A tree in a tray, and a decades-long argument with it about its shape.

nodes.label: Terrariums
nodes.blurb: A sealed jar with its own weather. Built in an afternoon, then watched for months to see if the moss agrees with your decisions.

nodes.label: Succulents and Cacti
nodes.blurb: Plants that thrive on neglect, killed most often by kindness. The gateway collection, one windowsill wide.

nodes.label: Orchids
nodes.blurb: Bark instead of soil, roots that want air and a bloom that takes a year to repeat. The difficulty setting above houseplants.

nodes.label: Composting
nodes.blurb: Greens, browns and a pile that either heats up or does not. Turning kitchen waste into next spring is slow alchemy with a fork.

nodes.label: Seed Saving
nodes.blurb: Envelopes, dates and which tomato crossed with which. A private seed bank grows out of one good season.

nodes.label: Propagation
nodes.blurb: Cuttings in water jars along the windowsill. The moment a plant becomes plants, and the reason nobody here buys them anymore.

nodes.label: Hydroponics
nodes.blurb: Pumps, nutrient solution and roots that never touch soil. A garden run on numbers: pH, EC and a timer doing the remembering.

nodes.label: Aquascaping
nodes.blurb: An underwater garden with CO2 injection and trimming scissors. Gardening at its most gear-heavy, judged like bonsai.

nodes.label: Garden Design
nodes.blurb: Borders, sight lines and what blooms after what. Planning in winter for a picture that only exists next August.

nodes.label: Wildlife Gardening
nodes.blurb: Ponds, log piles and plants chosen for who visits them. The garden becomes a habitat, and the gardener becomes an observer.

nodes.label: Home Cooking
nodes.blurb: Dinner, but on purpose. It stops being a chore roughly when you start cooking things nobody asked for.

nodes.label: Baking
nodes.blurb: Grams, oven temperatures and chemistry that shows its work. The branch of cooking where improvising is how things go wrong.

nodes.label: Sourdough
nodes.blurb: A jar of flour and water with a name. Feeding schedules, crumb photographs and a starter that outlives most gym memberships.

nodes.label: Fermentation
nodes.blurb: Kimchi, kraut, miso and things bubbling in jars. Controlled spoilage, run by people who read the funk like a weather report.

nodes.label: BBQ and Smoking
nodes.blurb: Fire management, rubs and a thermometer with wifi. Twelve hours for one meal, most of it spent watching a number not move.

nodes.label: Knife Skills
nodes.blurb: Grip, angle and a stone kept flat. Sharpening becomes its own hobby about a week after the first proper knife arrives.

nodes.label: Pasta Making
nodes.blurb: Flour, eggs and a crank machine bolted to the table. Shapes have names, regions and rules, and the dried stuff stops being acceptable.

nodes.label: Preserving
nodes.blurb: Jam, pickles and rows of labelled jars. Seasonal gluts turned shelf-stable, plus a working knowledge of botulism you did not plan on.

nodes.label: Homebrewing
nodes.blurb: Malt, yeast and sanitising everything twice. Five gallons at a time, with a hydrometer doing the scoring.

nodes.label: Bean-to-Bar Chocolate
nodes.blurb: Roasting cocoa, grinding it for two days and tempering by degrees. A hobby with one ingredient and a dozen ways to ruin it.

nodes.label: Food Photography
nodes.blurb: Plating, window light and a dinner going cold on purpose. The dish is finished when the shot is, not before.

nodes.label: Spice Blending
nodes.blurb: Whole seeds, a dry pan and a grinder that no longer does coffee. Garam masala from scratch recalibrates what the shop jars taste like.

nodes.label: Meal Planning
nodes.blurb: A week of dinners decided on Sunday. Spreadsheets, batch cooking and the quiet satisfaction of a freezer with an index.

nodes.label: Cheesemaking
nodes.blurb: Cultures, rennet and a curd you cut with a ruler. Fresh cheeses land in a weekend; the aged ones require a cave and a personality change.

nodes.label: Hiking
nodes.blurb: Boots, a route and a summit or a loop. The entry point to everything else out here, and the one that needs the least explaining.

nodes.label: Camping
nodes.blurb: A tent, a stove and a site picked off a map. Sleeping outside on purpose, with gear arguments to fill the winter.

nodes.label: Backpacking
nodes.blurb: Multi-day routes with everything on your back. The hobby where cutting the handle off a toothbrush counts as progress.

nodes.label: Bouldering
nodes.blurb: Short climbs, big pads and no rope. A puzzle you solve with your whole body, four metres off the ground.

nodes.label: Cycling
nodes.blurb: Road, gravel or trail, plus the maintenance stand in the hallway. The rule about how many bikes you need is not a joke to anyone here.

nodes.label: Birdwatching
nodes.blurb: Binoculars, a field guide and a life list. Starts with a robin at the feeder and ends with a dawn drive for a rare gull.

nodes.label: Fishing
nodes.blurb: Knots, casts and reading the water. Long stretches of nothing punctuated by the only part anyone photographs.

nodes.label: Foraging
nodes.blurb: Mushrooms, berries and hedgerow greens, identified twice before eaten once. The field guide is not optional.

nodes.label: Geocaching
nodes.blurb: GPS coordinates, a hidden box and a logbook to sign. A worldwide treasure hunt hiding in plain sight in every park.

nodes.label: Kayaking
nodes.blurb: Paddle strokes, launch points and reading a river. The boat on the car roof announces the hobby before you do.

nodes.label: Trail Running
nodes.blurb: Running where the ground argues back. Ankles, gels and elevation profiles studied like sheet music.

nodes.label: Field Sketching
nodes.blurb: A pocket watercolour set and a folding stool. Drawing the landscape fixes it in memory in a way the phone photo never has.

nodes.label: Weather Watching
nodes.blurb: Cloud atlases, pressure trends and a home station on the fence post. The forecast stops being something you receive.

nodes.label: Maps and Navigation
nodes.blurb: Contour lines, a compass bearing and no battery involved. The skill that turns a bad forecast into a story instead of a rescue.

nodes.label: Mystery and crime
nodes.blurb: A body, a detective and a fair chance to guess first. The genre with the strictest contract, read by people who audit every clause.

nodes.label: Horror
nodes.blurb: Ghosts, bad houses and things best left unnamed. Fans will explain it is really about grief, while enjoying the monster very much.

nodes.label: Historical fiction
nodes.blurb: Fiction wearing period dress, footnotes optional. Half the audience comes for the story and half comes to mark the author's homework.

nodes.label: Romance
nodes.blurb: The only genre that guarantees its ending and outsells the rest anyway. Apparently suspense was never about how it ends.

nodes.label: Literary fiction
nodes.blurb: Prize lists, sentence-level ambition and no promises about plot. The shelf where not finishing the book can still count as reading it.

nodes.label: Translated fiction
nodes.blurb: Someone rewrote every sentence so you could read it, and got a line on the title page for it. The prize stickers rarely mention them either.

nodes.label: Short stories
nodes.blurb: Whole worlds opened and closed inside twenty pages. The form everyone praises, teaches and recommends, and somehow never buys.

nodes.label: Doorstop epics
nodes.blurb: A thousand pages, three maps and a family tree. Starting one is less like choosing a book and more like signing a lease.

nodes.label: Rereading favourites
nodes.blurb: Back to the same shelf on purpose, sometimes on a schedule. Comfort, mostly, plus the quiet thrill of knowing the twist and watching it come.

nodes.label: Logs and reviews
nodes.blurb: Stars, spreadsheets and a running yearly count. The paper trail starts as a record of the reading and ends up assigning it.

nodes.label: Dialling in by taste
nodes.blurb: Change one brewing variable and compare the result. Notes connect what you did with what you actually enjoyed in the cup.

nodes.label: Puck preparation
nodes.blurb: Distribution and a repeatable routine before brewing. The useful goal is consistency between cups, not an elaborate ritual for its own sake.

nodes.label: Comparative tasting
nodes.blurb: Compare two cups and describe the difference in your own words. Sweetness, texture, and finish are more useful than guessing a flavour correctly.

nodes.label: Milk drinks
nodes.blurb: The balance between coffee, milk, and texture. A familiar drink becomes a way to notice how the ingredients change one another.

nodes.label: A brew journal
nodes.blurb: Dose, output, beans, and a short tasting note. Keep only the details that help you repeat a cup you liked.

nodes.label: Exploring coffee origins
nodes.blurb: Compare coffees while keeping your routine familiar. Origin, processing, and roast become questions you can investigate through taste.

nodes.label: Grit progression
nodes.blurb: Never skip a grit. One stray coarse grain leaves a scratch the next four grades cannot reach, whether you are sanding a seam or grinding a mirror.

nodes.label: Cutting
nodes.blurb: Knife, saw, nippers and shears. A sharp tool cuts where you aimed; a blunt one goes wherever the material prefers.

nodes.label: Drilling
nodes.blurb: Centre punch, pilot hole, then size. Skipping the punch is how a bit walks across a part you had finished.

nodes.label: Adhesives
nodes.blurb: Solvent, cyanoacrylate, epoxy and contact cement, each with a material it works on and several it ruins.

nodes.label: Filling
nodes.blurb: Putty, sand, inspect, repeat. Almost always more cycles than you planned, and the primer decides when you are done.

nodes.label: Measuring
nodes.blurb: Calipers, squares and a datum you keep returning to. Measuring from the last cut accumulates every error you made.

nodes.label: Jigs and clamps
nodes.blurb: The fixture that makes the second one match the first. Building the jig is usually faster than fixing the mismatch.

nodes.label: Dust and PPE
nodes.blurb: Extraction, eye protection and the right cartridge. Resin and MDF dust are the two most commonly skipped gates on this map.

nodes.label: Brush control
nodes.blurb: Thin your paint, load the tip, and pull the stroke. Every other technique is this one repeated with intent.

nodes.label: Priming
nodes.blurb: Adhesion, and a single flat colour that reveals every flaw the bare surface was hiding.

nodes.label: Airbrushing
nodes.blurb: Compressor, needle, air pressure. The gate on gradients, on modulation and on any finish that has to be even.

nodes.label: Masking
nodes.blurb: Tape, putty and film. A hard edge is not painted, it is lifted off afterwards.

nodes.label: Washes
nodes.blurb: Thinned dark paint pulled into the recesses over a gloss coat, then wiped back off the flats.

nodes.label: Highlighting
nodes.blurb: Edge highlights, layering and blending. Painting where the light would have been rather than where the colour is.

nodes.label: Weathering
nodes.blurb: Chipping, streaking, pigments and soot. Damage applied on purpose so the object reads as used.

nodes.label: Metallics
nodes.blurb: Metal paints, and the harder trick of painting non-metallic metal so a flat surface reads as polished steel.

nodes.label: Spray safety
nodes.blurb: Booth, extraction and a respirator with the right cartridge. Not optional the moment solvents are in the air.

nodes.label: Colour theory
nodes.blurb: Why a repaint looks better than the box art. Value first, then temperature, then saturation.

nodes.label: Composition
nodes.blurb: Position, framing, and the choice to leave something out. The same subject can tell very different stories from a step to the left.

nodes.label: Natural light
nodes.blurb: Window light, shade, and the short intervals when ordinary places look different. Learn to notice the light before choosing the settings.

nodes.label: Street photography
nodes.blurb: Gestures, layers, and fleeting arrangements in shared places. Observation and respect for the people around you are part of the practice.

nodes.label: Close-up photography
nodes.blurb: Small subjects become landscapes. Working distance, steady framing, and light matter as much as magnification.

nodes.label: Portraits
nodes.blurb: A photograph made with someone, rather than simply of them. Expression, comfort, and where the light falls all shape the result.

nodes.label: Photo essays
nodes.blurb: A set of pictures that says more than a single frame. Sequence, repetition, and the image you decide to remove become the work.

nodes.label: Automation Scripts
nodes.blurb: Rename five hundred files, scrape a page, wire two tools together. The door most hobbies enter through.

nodes.label: Web Design
nodes.blurb: HTML, CSS and restraint. A page that loads fast and says one thing well beats a framework you fight.

nodes.label: Microcontroller Code
nodes.blurb: Code with pins attached. Timing, memory and power budgets the desktop never made you think about.

nodes.label: Chatbots and Agents
nodes.blurb: Prompting, wiring and guardrails around a model someone else trained. The newest door, and the easiest to overestimate.

nodes.label: Journaling
nodes.blurb: Write down a small detail from the day and why it stayed with you. A record becomes a source of ideas without needing an audience.

nodes.label: Short fiction
nodes.blurb: A character wants something, and something resists. A short form lets you explore one turn in a life without inventing the whole world first.

nodes.label: Poetry experiments
nodes.blurb: Sound, rhythm, and the work a line break can do. Try a constraint and see which unexpected phrase it helps you find.

nodes.label: Worldbuilding
nodes.blurb: Imagine how a place works through its customs, materials, and ordinary routines. Details matter when they change what someone can do there.

nodes.label: Revision and editing
nodes.blurb: Read for one question at a time: meaning, structure, then the sentence. A finished draft is material to work with, rather than a verdict.

nodes.label: Writing useful instructions
nodes.blurb: Explain a small task to someone who has not done it. Their questions reveal the steps that felt too obvious to mention.

nodes.label: Flash removal
nodes.blurb: Trimming the casting seams and pour stubs. Resin dust is the part nobody warns a collector about, so wet sand it.

nodes.label: Pinning
nodes.blurb: Brass rod and a pin vise through both halves of a joint. Resin is heavy and a butt joint will fail, usually while somebody is holding it.

nodes.label: Degreasing
nodes.blurb: An overnight soak, a rinse and an ultrasonic clean to remove mould release. It is invisible, and skipping it lifts the paint weeks later.

nodes.label: Priming
nodes.blurb: A light mist coat, then a heavier one. The first primer layer shows every flaw that bare resin was hiding.

nodes.label: Pinhole repair
nodes.blurb: Bubbles that extend below the surface, so filling the top does not fix them. This is where the time actually goes.

nodes.label: Skin tones
nodes.blurb: The base coat that decides how the whole figure reads. Airbrushed in thin layers, warm in the shadows rather than grey.

nodes.label: Face and eyes
nodes.blurb: The single hardest step, and it has to happen before the hair goes on because the hair blocks access permanently.

nodes.label: Hair assembly
nodes.blurb: Puttied seams, then reprimed and repainted locally. Assembly and painting stop being separate stages here.

nodes.label: Gloss and flat
nodes.blurb: Gloss to carry a wash, flat to finish. Two different jobs that people mistake for one preference.

nodes.label: Slasher
nodes.blurb: A killer, a group and a body count. The most formalised structure in the genre, and the easiest to see broken on purpose.

nodes.label: Giallo
nodes.blurb: Italian, gloved, and lit in colours no room has ever been. Style as the point rather than as decoration.

nodes.label: Folk Horror
nodes.blurb: Landscape, old custom and a community that is not going to help you. Daylight is not a comfort here.

nodes.label: Cosmic Horror
nodes.blurb: The threat is scale, not intent. Adapts badly and often, which is half of what makes it interesting to follow.

nodes.label: Body Horror
nodes.blurb: Transformation, prosthetics and practical effects doing work no render has matched. The subgenre most tied to a craft.

nodes.label: Found Footage
nodes.blurb: A camera inside the story. Cheap enough that anyone can attempt it, which is why the range in quality is enormous.

nodes.label: Creature Feature
nodes.blurb: Something large and hostile, built in a workshop. The direct ancestor of every suit and every animatronic.

nodes.label: J-Horror
nodes.blurb: Quiet, domestic, and about the wrong thing being in the room with you. Reshaped the whole genre after 1998.

nodes.label: Parts picking
nodes.blurb: Compatibility lists, price history and a spreadsheet before any order. Most of the hobby happens before anything ships.

nodes.label: Watercooling
nodes.blurb: Blocks, radiators and tubing, soft or hard, up to a full custom loop. The leak test costs a day, and skipping it can cost a GPU.

nodes.label: Cable management
nodes.blurb: Routing, combs and velcro behind the motherboard tray. Invisible once the panel is on, which is exactly why it gets done properly.

nodes.label: Overclocking
nodes.blurb: More clock for more voltage until it stops being free. The stability testing is the hobby; the benchmark run is just the receipt.

nodes.label: Undervolting
nodes.blurb: The same curve worked in the other direction. Less heat and less noise for the same frames, and it costs nothing but an evening.

nodes.label: Small form factor
nodes.blurb: The whole machine in ten litres or less. Every part is chosen twice: once for performance, once for whether it physically fits.

nodes.label: Benchmarking
nodes.blurb: Runs, graphs and one percent lows. The machine was built to play games and then spends its first week being measured instead.

nodes.label: Silent builds
nodes.blurb: Fan curves, oversized heatsinks and rubber mounts. The finish line is a machine you have to look at to know it is on.

nodes.label: Case modding
nodes.blurb: Cut panels, custom paint and parts no catalogue sells. The point where a computer stops being assembled and starts being made.

nodes.label: Nursery stock hunting
nodes.blurb: Garden centres walked slowly, looking at trunks instead of foliage. The cheapest shrub on the rack sometimes hides the best tree, which is the whole sport.

nodes.label: Yamadori
nodes.blurb: Collecting wild trees, with permission, from mountains and hedgerows. Decades of natural struggle in one trunk, and a survival rate that teaches humility.

nodes.label: Wiring
nodes.blurb: Copper or aluminium wrapped along every branch to set its line. Hours of application, months of waiting, and one season too long leaves scars.

nodes.label: Pruning and ramification
nodes.blurb: Cut back, let it grow, cut back again until the twigs divide like a river delta. Most of the work is choosing what the tree loses.

nodes.label: Repotting and root work
nodes.blurb: Root pruning and fresh soil on a schedule the tree sets. A spring job with a short window, missed at the cost of a year.

nodes.label: Soil mixes
nodes.blurb: Akadama, pumice and lava, sieved into grades. Bags of imported clay, bought by people who own a garden full of free dirt.

nodes.label: Deadwood, jin and shari
nodes.blurb: Dead branches and stripped trunk, carved and bleached with lime sulphur. Making part of a tree look dead takes surprising care with the living part.

nodes.label: Species study
nodes.blurb: Junipers, maples and ficus each want different work in different months. Knowing one species well beats owning ten confused trees.

nodes.label: Pots and display
nodes.blurb: The pot is half the picture, and collectors treat it that way. Stands, scrolls and accent plants turn a tree into an exhibit.

nodes.label: Winter care
nodes.blurb: Cold frames, mulched pots and roots that freeze faster in a tray than in the ground. The quiet season, which the trees do not consider optional.

nodes.label: Reading the light
nodes.blurb: Track where the light reaches during the day and across seasons. The bright-looking corner and the useful growing spot are not always the same.

nodes.label: Watering observations
nodes.blurb: Notice the plant, pot, and moisture in the growing medium together. A routine starts with checking, rather than watering by a fixed calendar.

nodes.label: Propagation experiments
nodes.blurb: Learn how a particular species makes new plants and document one attempt. Labels and dates help you notice slow changes.

nodes.label: Pots and growing media
nodes.blurb: Roots, drainage, and the material around them. Container choices make more sense when you know how the particular plant grows.

nodes.label: A plant journal
nodes.blurb: Photographs, dates, and small observations collected over time. The new leaf is easier to appreciate when you remember where it started.

nodes.label: Plant swaps
nodes.blurb: Share plants, cuttings, and the care notes that go with them. A conversation often tells you more than the label on the pot.

nodes.label: Cookies
nodes.blurb: Drop, slice-and-bake and the endless chocolate chip variations. The lowest stakes in baking, which is why everyone runs their most serious experiments here.

nodes.label: Cakes and sponges
nodes.blurb: Genoise, chiffon and the layer cake with a crumb coat. The first bake with an audience, since nobody makes a cake for no one.

nodes.label: Enriched doughs
nodes.blurb: Brioche, babka and cinnamon rolls, doughs with butter and eggs on the payroll. Slower to rise than anything else here, and gone faster.

nodes.label: Laminated pastry
nodes.blurb: Croissants and puff, butter folded into dough until the layers run to the hundreds. A kitchen two degrees too warm undoes an hour of work.

nodes.label: Pie and tart crust
nodes.blurb: Shortcrust, blind baking and the crimp that identifies the baker. Soggy bottoms are discussed with a seriousness outsiders find alarming.

nodes.label: Baker's percentages
nodes.blurb: Every ingredient written as a percentage of the flour. A notation change that quietly turns recipes into things you can reason about.

nodes.label: Starter keeping
nodes.blurb: Flour, water and a feeding schedule kept like a rota. Holidays now get planned around who minds the jar.

nodes.label: Rye and whole grain
nodes.blurb: Dense flours, thirsty doughs and flavours white flour never mentions. The crumb gets tighter and the opinions get stronger.

nodes.label: Bread scoring
nodes.blurb: A razor, a steady wrist and one committed stroke before the oven. Wheat stalks and spirals, drawn on a surface that will not sit still.

nodes.label: Oven steam tricks
nodes.blurb: Dutch ovens, lava rocks and a tray of boiling water on the bottom shelf. Domestic ovens vent steam out on purpose, so bakers spend years sneaking it back in.

nodes.label: Circuit simulation
nodes.blurb: Try a simple circuit virtually and inspect what each component contributes. A simulator gives ideas somewhere to fail without consuming parts.

nodes.label: Buttons and input
nodes.blurb: Give a project a button, then decide what a press means. A tiny interaction introduces state, timing, and feedback.

nodes.label: Reading sensors
nodes.blurb: Turn a measurement into a value you can inspect. Compare readings before making the project react to them.

nodes.label: Light and sound feedback
nodes.blurb: Use a small light or sound to communicate what a project is doing. Clear feedback can explain a device without a screen.

nodes.label: Serial debugging
nodes.blurb: Print what the code believes is happening, then compare it with the circuit. Small observations narrow a confusing fault to a question you can test.

nodes.label: A home for the project
nodes.blurb: Plan where the board, wires, and controls will sit. A cardboard mock-up reveals awkward button positions before you make anything permanent.

nodes.label: Panel lining
nodes.blurb: A wash into the recesses. The cheapest step with the largest visible return.

nodes.label: Top coat
nodes.blurb: Matt or gloss over the whole kit. Kills the toy shine and seals decals.

nodes.label: Weathering
nodes.blurb: Chipping, staining, exhaust soot. Deliberate damage that reads as history.

nodes.label: Scribing
nodes.blurb: Cutting your own panel lines. The first irreversible thing you do to a kit.

nodes.label: Nub removal
nodes.blurb: Cut proud of the part, then shave the stub. Cutting flush whitens the plastic and the mark never comes out.

nodes.label: Seam removal
nodes.blurb: Cement, cure, sand. Erasing the fact that the arm arrived as two halves.

nodes.label: Pla-plate work
nodes.blurb: Styrene sheet and rod added to a kit until the silhouette is yours rather than the box art's.

nodes.label: LED install
nodes.blurb: Drilling a head to light the eyes. The point where a plastic kit acquires a power switch.

nodes.label: Rhythm and strumming
nodes.blurb: A steady pulse and accents that give a song its shape. Muted strings are enough to practise a rhythm before adding chords.

nodes.label: Fingerstyle
nodes.blurb: Bass, melody, and accompaniment shared between the fingers. Slow, separate patterns eventually become one moving part.

nodes.label: Learning by ear
nodes.blurb: Finding a melody or chord change by listening and trying it. Short phrases and repetition turn a recording into a conversation.

nodes.label: Writing songs
nodes.blurb: A chord loop, a phrase, or a rhythm that keeps coming back. Record small ideas so they have somewhere to meet later.

nodes.label: Improvisation
nodes.blurb: Making a phrase and answering it in real time. A few notes used deliberately can carry more than an uninterrupted run of scales.

nodes.label: Playing together
nodes.blurb: Listening while you play, leaving room, and recovering together when the timing slips. The arrangement changes with the people in the room.

nodes.label: Field notes
nodes.blurb: Record shape, posture, movement, and habitat before looking up a name. An uncertain observation is still useful when its details are clear.

nodes.label: Listening for birds
nodes.blurb: Separate the sounds around you and describe a rhythm or repeated phrase. Listening adds another layer to a place you already know.

nodes.label: A regular observation spot
nodes.blurb: Return to one accessible place across different days and seasons. Familiarity makes small changes visible.

nodes.label: Watching behaviour
nodes.blurb: Feeding, resting, and interactions tell stories beyond identification. Keep enough distance that your presence does not change what you are watching.

nodes.label: Bird sketches
nodes.blurb: Quick shapes and notes record what caught your attention. The drawing is a way to look more carefully, not an illustration contest.

nodes.label: Seasonal observations
nodes.blurb: Keep dates and locations for the changes you notice. Over time, a familiar place gains a calendar of its own.

nodes.label: Day hikes
nodes.blurb: Up in the morning, back for dinner, one summit or a loop. The format everything else on this map quietly complicates.

nodes.label: Overnight and thru routes
nodes.blurb: The walk keeps going after dark, so the house comes along. Somewhere past the second night it stops being a hike and becomes a commute with views.

nodes.label: Map and compass
nodes.blurb: Contours, bearings and a plastic baseplate that never needs charging. Practised on clear days so it works on the day the cloud comes down.

nodes.label: GPX planning
nodes.blurb: Routes drawn at a desk the week before, elevation profile and all. Some of a walk's best hours happen at the computer, which nobody admits.

nodes.label: Trail snacks and water
nodes.blurb: Calories per gram, litres per hour and a firm position on jelly sweets. The menu gets planned harder than most dinner parties.

nodes.label: Footwear and blister craft
nodes.blurb: Boots or trail shoes, lacing patterns and tape applied before the hot spot, not after. Feet are the one piece of gear you cannot swap mid-walk.

nodes.label: Peak bagging
nodes.blurb: A published list of summits and a tick against each one. The hill was always there; the spreadsheet is what gets you out in November.

nodes.label: Night hikes
nodes.blurb: The same trail after dark, on a headtorch beam. Familiar paths stop being familiar, which is either the appeal or the warning.

nodes.label: Leave no trace
nodes.blurb: Pack it out, keep to the path, leave nothing to find. The one discipline here that is invisible when done well, which makes it hard to show off.

nodes.label: Hiking logs
nodes.blurb: Dates, routes, weather and who came along, kept for years. Reads as admin until the day you need to know which year the bridge washed out.

nodes.label: Dipole
nodes.blurb: Two legs of wire and a feedpoint. The first antenna most people build and the one that keeps working.

nodes.label: Vertical
nodes.blurb: A quarter wave against a ground plane. Low angle radiation, and a radial field you will never finish laying.

nodes.label: Yagi
nodes.blurb: A driven element plus directors and a reflector. Gain in one direction, which means you now need a rotator.

nodes.label: Magnetic loop
nodes.blurb: A tuned loop small enough for a balcony. Narrow bandwidth, high voltage at the capacitor, quiet on receive.

nodes.label: SWR and tune
nodes.blurb: Measuring how much power is coming back instead of leaving. Trim, measure, trim again, and never guess.

nodes.label: Feedline
nodes.blurb: Coax, ladder line, connectors and the loss you accept between the rig and the wire.

nodes.label: Addressing
nodes.blurb: Giving each locomotive a number the command station calls it by. The step that makes two trains on one track possible at all.

nodes.label: CV programming
nodes.blurb: Configuration variables for momentum, speed curves and lighting. A decoder's whole personality lives in a table of numbers.

nodes.label: Consisting
nodes.blurb: Two or more locomotives responding as one, with speed matching so they do not fight each other on a grade.

nodes.label: Sound decoders
nodes.blurb: A speaker in a space that has no room for one, plus an enclosure, because a bare speaker in a shell sounds like a phone.

nodes.label: Block detection
nodes.blurb: The layout knowing where trains are. The prerequisite for signals and for anything automatic.

nodes.label: Computer control
nodes.blurb: Open software driving the railway: rosters, throttles, signalling and dispatch, from a laptop on the fascia.

nodes.label: Throttles
nodes.blurb: Tethered, radio or a phone. What visiting operators actually touch, and the part they will have opinions about.

nodes.label: Track plan
nodes.blurb: What the railway is for, drawn as track. A plan with a purpose survives contact with a room; a plan that is only a shape does not.

nodes.label: Minimum radius
nodes.blurb: The tightest curve on the layout decides what will ever run on it. Long stock on a tight curve derails and keeps derailing.

nodes.label: Staging
nodes.blurb: Hidden tracks where trains come from and go to. Without it the railway is a loop; with it, it is part of a network.

nodes.label: Helix
nodes.blurb: A spiral to get between levels. Eats an enormous amount of space and run length to gain one deck.

nodes.label: Grades
nodes.blurb: How steeply track can climb before a locomotive stalls with a realistic train behind it. Two percent is already a lot.

nodes.label: Aisle width
nodes.blurb: Where the people stand. Designed last by beginners and first by anybody who has run an operating session.

nodes.label: Backdrop
nodes.blurb: The painted sky behind the scenery. Removes the corner of the room from every photograph you will ever take.

nodes.label: Layout lighting
nodes.blurb: Even, colour-correct light over the whole layout. Changes how the scenery reads more than another month of scenery would.

nodes.label: Saber hilt
nodes.blurb: Machined or kit-built aluminium, greeblied, finished and drilled for a chassis. The build the other five steps were for.

nodes.label: Blaster
nodes.blurb: A resin or printed shell built on the silhouette of a real firearm somebody dressed in 1976.

nodes.label: Helmet
nodes.blurb: Vac-formed or printed, then sanded through grits until the print lines are gone. The part a club will judge hardest.

nodes.label: Armour
nodes.blurb: ABS or foam panels trimmed to a body that is not the reference body. Strapping is the half nobody photographs.

nodes.label: Greeblies
nodes.blurb: The found parts glued on for texture. Half of prop accuracy is identifying which calculator the original came from.

nodes.label: Prop finishing
nodes.blurb: Anodising, paint, and weathering that matches a screen-used object rather than a factory one.

nodes.label: Cooperative play
nodes.blurb: Work together against the game and talk through a shared problem. The challenge includes making room for everyone at the table to decide.

nodes.label: Deck building
nodes.blurb: Your available actions change as you assemble a deck during play. Each new card asks what you want the next few turns to become.

nodes.label: Worker placement
nodes.blurb: A limited number of actions and places that other players can occupy first. Timing and opportunity cost give an ordinary-looking choice its weight.

nodes.label: Abstract strategy
nodes.blurb: A small set of rules and a position you can read together. Depth comes from how simple moves change the possibilities for both players.

nodes.label: Party and word games
nodes.blurb: Clues, associations, and the different ways people understand the same prompt. The conversation can be as memorable as the result.

nodes.label: Solo puzzles and scenarios
nodes.blurb: A puzzle or unfolding scenario at your own pace. Replaying can reveal a different decision rather than simply a better result.

nodes.label: Assembly cut
nodes.blurb: Everything usable in order, far too long. You cannot judge structure until the whole thing exists badly.

nodes.label: Pacing
nodes.blurb: Cutting the parts you enjoyed making. The single largest difference between a build log and a video.

nodes.label: B-roll
nodes.blurb: Cutaways that cover a jump and show the detail. Shot after the edit exists, once you know what is missing.

nodes.label: Sound mix
nodes.blurb: Levels, music under voice, and room tone under silence. Viewers forgive a soft picture and leave over bad sound.

nodes.label: Titles
nodes.blurb: Names, labels and the number that tells somebody which part they are on. Small, and usually the last thing done.

nodes.label: Captions
nodes.blurb: Burned in or as a track. Half of all viewing is muted, and captions are how a deaf viewer gets in at all.

nodes.label: Proxies
nodes.blurb: Editing against small copies so the timeline scrubs, then relinking to the originals to export. A workflow, not a setting.
